messages.subject: modeling density estimates
parts:
Hi all, I have asked this question previously, but it has been awhile so =
I=20
thought I'd ask again.

I have distance sampling data from avian point count surveys in areas=20
treated by prescribed fire and untreated areas. I would like to relate=20=

habitat characteristics at the level of the point count to density=20
estimates at the point count. Obviously, I would need to pool data to=20
estimate a detection function to get the density estimates for each=20
individual point count. It is my understanding that there are a variety =
of=20
statistical issues associated with conducting this type of analysis.=20=20=


I know there are papers by Royle addressing this issue, but I'm confused=20=

about whether the methods suggested by Royle in Ecology 2004 are=20
appropriate for my data or if there are other methods that are more=20
appropriate.

Perhaps this analysis is not as complicated as I was lead to believe?

Any help on the matter would be appreciated.

Thanks,

Robin Russell

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: modeling density estimates
parts:
I thought I answered this one or one like it awhile back, The method
proposed by Royle et al would work for what you want to do. The only
statistical issue is in coping with the uncertainty associated with
estimation of the detection probability in the evaluation of the density
affect. However, in your case this is relatively straightforward as
long as you estimate detection probability separately for the treatment
(fire) and control areas. Then you can construct 2 independent
estimates of D with std errors that incorporate both variation due to
sampling and estimation of detection probability. You can construct an
approximate z-test as (Dfire - Dcontrol)/sqrt(var(Dfire) +
var(Dcontrol)). If your df are small you may want to use the
Satterthwaite approximation and construct a pooled df and use a t-test
in evaluating the hypothesis. Or if you prefer, you can estimate the
effect size as Dfire-Dcontrol and its std error is simply
sqrt(var(Dfire) + var(Dcontrol)). If the individual cvs are large then
you may want to use the log normal approach instead rather than the
normality assumption. It becomes trickier if you have a common
detection function but even than can be handled in the case of
trt-control. What gets messier is more than one level for the treatment
or multiple covariate effects. That is where the method proposed by
Royle et al will be better and frames the analysis in a model selection
approach with a likelihood for abundance as well as detection. There is
a considerable amount of work being done on this subject and eventuallly
software will follow. For the time being what I've described above may
work for your situation.

regards --jeff
